 AI Summary 
 Coinbase blocked $4.7 million in user transfers linked to a cryptocurrency scam that used an artificial intelligence deepfake video of Elon Musk, preventing funds from leaving before losses occurred. The scammers hijacked a YouTube live broadcast of a Tesla “flying car” demonstration and displayed a QR code urging viewers to send crypto for a promised double return. More than 500,000 viewers joined the fake stream, Coinbase said.

 This case shows how quickly scams can spread when deepfakes are combined with live streams on major platforms. [Photo: ChatGPT] 
 Coinbase prevented the outflow of $4.7 million in user funds in a cryptocurrency scam that used a deepfake video of Elon Musk. As scams spread that combine celebrity videos with fake cryptocurrency giveaways, the exchange's automated security system blocked transfers before losses occurred.
 Cryptopolitan, a blockchain media outlet, reported on Nov. 18 that the scammers hijacked a YouTube live broadcast of what it called a Tesla "flying car" demonstration and then aired an artificial intelligence deepfake video of Musk. The video promoted a giveaway event promising to return double the amount of cryptocurrency sent, and it displayed a QR code to prompt viewers to transfer funds.
 More than 500,000 people flocked to the fake livestream. Coinbase said that over about 2 hours, hundreds of its users tried to send millions of dollars to the attackers' wallet, but its automated defense system blocked about 91 percent of those attempts without employee intervention. The blocked amount totaled $4.7 million.
 The scam is a typical giveaway scheme that exploits a celebrity's credibility to induce users to transfer cryptocurrency themselves. It lowered viewers' guard by combining a deepfake video of Musk with a large-scale livestream, and it simplified the transfer process through a QR code.
 The scale of cryptocurrency crime is also growing. DefiLlama data show 343 cryptocurrency theft incidents so far this year, with losses reaching $8.78 billion. A hacking case related to Binance in October had a significant impact on the loss figure, and investigative authorities identified the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor as being behind what they said was the largest cryptocurrency theft in history.
 Scams using deepfakes are also rising rapidly. TRM Labs said in August that reported losses from deepfake scams in 2026 had already increased 263 percent compared with the full-year total for 2025. Unlike hacking that attacks system vulnerabilities, scams that directly deceive users into sending funds are increasing the importance of exchanges' transaction monitoring and transfer-blocking capabilities.
 Coinbase has responded before to cryptocurrency scams that used Musk. In July 2020, Twitter accounts of Musk and other celebrities were hacked and scam posts were uploaded promising to return a larger amount if cryptocurrency was sent. At the time, Coinbase manually blocked the bitcoin addresses used by the scammers, but the response was closer to an after-the-fact measure taken after checking disclosed addresses.
 This time, the response differed in that an automated system detected users' transfer attempts and blocked them before funds were drained. The scam method is not much different from 6 years ago, but it has evolved from posts on hijacked accounts to sophisticated deepfake videos, and a single livestream can now reach hundreds of thousands of people.
 As the cost of producing deepfakes falls and videos become more sophisticated, cryptocurrency scams using celebrities are increasingly likely to spread further. The role of exchange security is also expanding from tracking losses that have already occurred to detecting and blocking suspicious transfers by users in advance.
